description:
I’m here to make a microchip think like a mission commander.

I'm a young innovator obsessed with aerospace engineering, intelligent propulsion, microelectronics, and making the impossible computationally possible. I'm already developing a micro-scale propulsion system and microchip optimization technology now I'm taking that ambition to NASA Space Apps.
summary:
Meet NŪR GeoShadow-X, our African-inspired, AI-powered lunar mission intelligence platform, transforming NASA's open scientific resources into an interactive landing-site and energy-survival simulator.

We engineered a Python-based, physics-guided computer-vision system integrating NASA's LROC imagery, LOLA's five-meter-resolution topographic models, and JPL Horizons' Sun–Earth positioning data. Our custom 148,662-parameter neural network combines seven input channels, dual image–terrain encoders, cross-modal attention, and geometric ray tracing to predict lunar shadows and identify uncertain regions.

We documented our architecture, mathematical models, experiments, and statistical findings in a complete scientific research paper. Our prototype achieved 98.85% Intersection over Union across 19 held-out synthetic lunar scenes, establishing a computational proof of concept before validation on real NASA imagery.

But we went further. We connected GeoShadow-X to a lunar microgrid simulation, exploring how extreme south-polar shading affects solar generation, battery reserves, and spacecraft operations.

Through an intuitive, game-like interface, users can investigate landing scenarios and their engineering trade-offs, making sophisticated lunar research accessible to students, educators, and mission planners.

NŪR: Find the light. Protect the power.
details:
NUR, which stands for Navigate Under Radiance, helps people explore how landing location and arrival time affect a spacecraft’s operations on the Moon. Developed by Team WYYACK, our project brings together an interactive mission planner, a first-person lunar landing game and research into shadow detection. We want users to understand why reaching the surface safely is only part of the challenge. A spacecraft still needs enough sunlight to generate power and a clear view of Earth to communicate.

Users begin by exploring a lunar map, selecting a region or entering coordinates, and choosing a mission date and duration. They can compare up to three scenarios and examine how the Sun and Earth move relative to the surrounding horizon. This makes it possible to explore practical questions: What changes if the mission arrives two weeks later? How long could nearby terrain block sunlight? When might Earth disappear from view?

The game lets users experience the consequences of those choices. After planning their mission, they control a spacecraft’s descent, manage thrust and sideways drift, and attempt a safe landing. Surface operations then introduce another set of decisions. Running scientific instruments consumes energy, transmitting data depends on Earth visibility, and entering hibernation reduces power demand. A successful landing can therefore lead to a difficult surface mission if the player overlooks the conditions that follow it.

We also included GeoShadowNet-Lite, a small neural network that runs inside the browser and examines simulated shadow patterns. Alongside this game component, our separate GeoShadow-X research prototype explores how image features can be combined with terrain information and a physics-based shadow estimate. Its purpose is to investigate shadow detection while highlighting areas where the available evidence is uncertain. In the research paper’s evaluation on 19 held-out synthetic scenes, GeoShadow-X achieved a shadow intersection-over-union score of 0.9885. This measures overlap between predicted and reference shadows. The result comes from generated data; performance on independently annotated lunar imagery still needs to be established.

NASA resources guide our scientific development. Our research identifies imagery from the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera, elevation and uncertainty products from the Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter, and Sun and Earth position data from NASA/JPL Horizons as inputs for a future verified workflow. Moon Trek also provides a reference for exploring lunar geography. The current playable game uses procedurally generated terrain and approximate astronomical calculations, so we label its scenarios as illustrative. Integrating and independently checking actual lunar datasets is an important next step.

We developed the browser experience using JavaScript, HTML and CSS, with Three.js for the 3D environment and esbuild for bundling. Our machine-learning work uses Python and PyTorch. The Web Audio API generates music and sound effects, while Kokoro provides synthetic mission-control voices. Subtitles, control instructions and visual indicators help users follow the experience. Claude supported coding and development. The game is designed for browser play, with the full 3D experience best explored on a laptop or desktop.

The creative connection in NUR is between planning a mission and living through its consequences. Users can examine a scenario, attempt the landing, discover an operational problem and return to their original decision with a better understanding of what matters. The research component gives interested users a further route into the methods and evidence behind shadow assessment.

Throughout development, we considered limited battery capacity, terrain obstruction, changing mission dates, data coverage and the difference between geometric Earth visibility and a reliable radio connection. We also considered how to explain these ideas without requiring specialist knowledge.

Our immediate intended impact is educational: helping students, educators and the public understand the decisions behind lunar exploration through an experience they can control. Over time, we aim to develop a more thoroughly validated comparison workspace that could support early research and engineering discussions. We want NUR to make those discussions easier to enter, while keeping the assumptions and evidence visible.
